screens.title: NoC Router Microarchitecture
screens.narratorSegment: A NoC router is the local traffic controller that moves flits from incoming links to outgoing links. At its simplest the router has input buffers where arriving flits are stored, a route computation unit that chooses an output port based on the packet destination and routing algorithm, a switch allocator that resolves contention when multiple inputs want the same output, and a crossbar that physically connects inputs to outputs for the transfer. Input buffers are sized to absorb bursts; a typical design uses 4–16 flits per input port. The switch allocator can use round-robin fairness or priority arbitration when latency-sensitive traffic exists. Crossbars are sized to the number of ports: for a 5-port router (north, south, east, west, local) a 5×5 crossbar provides full connectivity. Output buffers are optional — some designs use cut-through traversal to reduce latency by allowing flits to pass through without per-hop output buffering. An important misconception is to equate larger buffers with always better performance. In practice, larger buffers increase area and power and can hide backpressure poorly; sizing is a trade-off informed by expected traffic burstiness. Example: a router receiving short bursts from four neighbors benefits from moderate input buffers and a fair allocator to avoid starvation. Key takeaway: understand each block’s role so you can balance latency, throughput and area when sizing buffers and picking arbitration policies. How would you change buffer depth if burstiness doubled?

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.1 › Router Microarchitecture
NoC Router Microarchitecture
The key hardware blocks that move flits between ports.
Definition and roles
  • Input buffers: hold arriving flits; typical depth 4–16 flits.
  • Route computation: maps destination to output port using routing algorithm.
  • Switch allocator: arbitrates competing requests; round-robin or priority.
  • Crossbar: N×N fabric to connect inputs to outputs.
Example
A 5-port router (N,S,E,W,local) uses a 5×5 crossbar. If two inputs request the same output, the allocator grants one and the other waits in its input buffer.
Key Takeaway

Decompose a router into buffers, decision logic, arbitration and fabric. Each part contributes to latency, throughput and area.

An annotated microarchitecture panel
Input Buffers
Per-input buffers store flits; per-VC buffers if virtual channels are present.
Route Computation
Compute next hop using destination address and routing rules (e.g., XY routing).
Switch Allocator
Resolve conflicts; choose grant ordering and fairness policy.
Crossbar
Connects winners to outputs; traversal may be pipelined for timing.
Common misconception
Bigger buffers always increase performance. In reality larger buffers increase area and power and may hide systemic congestion instead of solving it; allocator fairness and routing decisions are equally important.

screens.title: Router Pipeline and Lookahead Routing
screens.narratorSegment: Routers commonly implement a simple pipeline to structure work and meet timing. The three-stage pipeline is: Buffer Write where an incoming flit is stored in an input buffer, Route Computation combined with Switch Allocation where the next-hop output and the switch grant are decided, and Switch Traversal plus Link Traversal where the flit crosses the crossbar and enters the physical link to the next router. This pipeline ensures predictable throughput but introduces per-hop latency. Lookahead routing is an optimization where a router computes the route for the next hop before the flit arrives at that hop. With lookahead, the downstream router can start its allocation in parallel, effectively reducing the pipeline depth seen per hop. For example, a design that normally takes three cycles per hop might be reduced to two cycles per hop with lookahead for single-flit packets. A common misconception is that lookahead always reduces latency without cost. In practice, lookahead increases control complexity and may require extra wiring or speculative state. Concrete example: with two-cycle-per-router lookahead and one cycle per link, a packet traversing 6 hops would take roughly 6×(2+1) minus lookahead overlaps; we reason carefully about overlaps when computing end-to-end latency. Takeaway: pipeline stages and lookahead trade simplicity for per-hop latency; choose based on packet sizes and timing budgets.

keyIdea.text: Router pipeline stages set per-hop latency; lookahead routing reduces visible per-hop latency at the cost of complexity.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.1 › Router Pipeline
Router Pipeline and Lookahead
How staging work affects latency and how lookahead can reduce visible per-hop cost.
1. Buffer Write (BW)
Incoming flit is written into the input buffer and awaits allocation.
→
2. Route Computation + Switch Allocation (RC/SA)
Compute output port and arbitrate grants among competing inputs.
→
3. Switch Traversal + Link Traversal (ST/LT)
Flit crosses the crossbar and is sent over the physical link to the next router.
Lookahead routing
Compute the next hop earlier so the downstream allocator can start work in parallel. This reduces effective cycles per hop but adds control complexity and possible speculative state management.
Why this matters
  • Pipeline depth determines per-hop latency and influences throughput under contention.
  • Lookahead shortens end-to-end latency for small packets at the expense of complexity.
  • Choose pipeline style based on target packet size and timing budget.
Check your understanding
If you have two-cycle router lookahead and one-cycle link, how many cycles for a 3-hop route? Consider overlap between lookahead stages when you answer.

screens.title: Virtual Channels and Their Uses
screens.narratorSegment: Virtual channels (VCs) are multiple logical buffers multiplexed over a single physical link. Each VC has its own buffer and flow-control state, which means we can separate traffic classes or protocol directions without adding extra physical wires. VCs solve several problems. First, they avoid deadlock by separating traffic into virtual networks that do not form cyclic dependencies; for example, separating request and reply packets into distinct VCs prevents a cycle where each packet waits on buffers held by the other. Second, VCs enable quality-of-service: a high-priority flow can use a dedicated VC so that low-priority traffic does not block it. Third, VCs reduce head-of-line blocking because if one VC's head flit is blocked, other VCs on the same physical link can still make progress. A typical router uses two to four VCs per input port. A common misconception is to treat VCs as a free win; in practice they increase area, buffering requirements and control complexity. Concrete example: two-packet deadlock where packets swap directions on adjacent routers can be resolved by allocating distinct VCs for those directions. Takeaway: VCs are a powerful, well-understood tool for deadlock avoidance and performance isolation, but they cost area and design complexity, so pick the number of VCs based on workload needs and power budgets.

keyIdea.text: Multiple logical buffers per link break dependency cycles, enable QoS, and reduce head-of-line blocking at the cost of area and control complexity.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.1 › Virtual Channels
Virtual Channels and Their Uses
Why VCs are used and what they buy you in a router.
What is a virtual channel?
A VC is a separate logical buffer and flow-control context multiplexed on a physical link; it provides isolation between packet streams.
Benefits
  • Deadlock avoidance by separating traffic into virtual networks.
  • Quality-of-service via dedicated VCs for high-priority flows.
  • Reduced head-of-line blocking so other VCs can progress when one is stalled.
Misconception
VCs do not come for free: more VCs require more buffers and control logic, increasing area and power. Choose VCs to balance isolation and cost.
Concrete example
Consider request and reply packets crossing the same link. If both use the same VC they can create a cyclic wait. Assign request packets to VC0 and replies to VC1 to prevent this cycle.
Quick visual
VC0 ─ requests
VC1 ─ replies
VC2 ─ priority traffic
VC3 ─ background
Key Takeaway

Use VCs to break dependency cycles and isolate flows, and budget area/power for the added buffers and control logic.

screens.title: VC Microarchitecture and Buffer Sizing
screens.narratorSegment: When you add virtual channels you change the router’s buffering structure: each input port now contains multiple VCs, and each VC has its own buffer and flow-control state. A typical design uses two to four VCs per input port; each VC buffer depth is often 4–16 flits depending on burstiness. Buffer sizing affects area and power directly because more buffer entries mean more SRAM or register file resources. To ground this, consider the hands-on design: a 4×4 mesh has 16 nodes. Each router in our example has 5 ports (north, south, east, west, local), 2 VCs per port, and 4 flits per VC. If one flit is 128 bits wide, calculate total buffer bits per router by multiplying ports × VCs × depth × flit width. Many students forget to multiply by the number of ports when counting buffers; this omission underestimates area and power. Practical tip: compute the per-router total and then scale to the full network to estimate aggregate buffer memory. Example calculation: 5 ports × 2 VCs × 4 flits × 128 bits = 5,120 bits per router. If you then multiply across 16 routers you get the full chip buffer bits. Key takeaway: buffer sizing is straightforward arithmetic but decisive for area and power budgets; always account for ports, VCs and flit width together.

keyIdea.title: Buffer sizing formula
keyIdea.text: Total buffer bits = ports × VCs per port × flits per VC × flit width; scale per router to the network.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.1 › VC Microarchitecture
VC Microarchitecture and Buffer Sizing
How to compute buffer bits and what matters when adding VCs.
Per-router buffer calculation
Use the formula: ports × VCs per port × flits per VC × flit width.
Example: 4×4 mesh router
Ports = 5
VCs per port = 2
Flits per VC = 4
Flit width = 128 bits

Total buffer bits per router = 5 × 2 × 4 × 128 = 5120 bits
Total routers = 16
Total chip buffer bits = 16 × 5120 = 81,920 bits
Common mistake
Forgetting to multiply by the number of ports or neglecting VC count underestimates buffer cost and power impact.
Design considerations
  • More VCs improve isolation but require more storage and control logic.
  • Depth trades off buffering for area and power; size to expected burst lengths.
  • Synthesizable SRAM or register files have area and timing differences—budget accordingly.
Pro Tip

Perform buffer sizing early in the design so routing and allocator choices can be co-optimized with memory area constraints.

screens.title: NoC Topologies: Ring, Mesh, Crossbar, Hierarchical
screens.narratorSegment: Selecting a NoC topology is a central design decision. A ring is simple and has low router count, so it can be efficient for small systems. However, its bandwidth across any bisection remains small, which limits throughput as the core count grows. A mesh is regular and scales to many cores: routers tile the chip and links are relatively short, and the mesh offers multiple independent paths so aggregate throughput increases with size. Crossbars give full connectivity within small clusters and provide very high bandwidth at small scale, but they become impractical beyond a few cores due to area and wiring. Hierarchical designs combine local rings or crossbars with a global mesh to get the best of both: local low-latency clusters and scalable global interconnect. When comparing these topologies, consider latency, throughput, power, and area. Common misconception: assume the mesh always outperforms the ring. For small N a ring may have lower average latency and lower power. Example: for N=16 cores a ring can be efficient, but for N=64 a mesh's increased bisection bandwidth becomes critical. Takeaway: match topology to expected core count and communication patterns; use hierarchical mixes when both local and global traffic matter.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.1 › NoC Topologies
NoC Topologies: Ring, Mesh, Crossbar, Hierarchical
Choose a layout based on scale and traffic patterns.
Ring
Simple, low router count and low area for small systems. Limited bisection bandwidth makes it unsuitable for manycore throughput needs.
Mesh
Regular layout, good scalability, multiple paths and improved bisection bandwidth. Average hop count grows with the square root of N in an N-node mesh arrangement.
Crossbar
Full bandwidth within a small cluster; area and wiring explode with core count so crossbars are used for small groups, not whole-chip interconnects.
Hierarchical
Combine local rings or crossbars with a global mesh to balance local latency and global throughput. Useful when workloads show locality clustered in small groups.
Design lens
Ask: what is the expected core count and communication pattern? If local traffic dominates, a hierarchical or clustered design can yield low latency and scalable bandwidth. If many-to-many traffic dominates, prefer mesh-like structures.

screens.title: Latency, Throughput, Power and Area Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: NoC design is a careful balance between latency, throughput, power and area. Latency depends on the average number of hops between source and destination and the router pipeline depth; meshes typically give O(√N) hops while rings can require O(N) hops. Throughput is governed by bisection bandwidth: meshes scale with the square root of the node count because multiple links cross the bisection, whereas a ring provides constant bisection bandwidth regardless of size. Power is driven by the number of routers, length and number of links, and the amount of buffering; meshes have more routers but shorter links, rings have fewer routers but longer links; both choices change dynamic and static power. Area is dominated by router logic and buffers — more VCs and deeper buffers increase area. Designers often trade a little extra latency for much higher throughput or lower power, depending on workload. For example, accepting O(√N) hops in a mesh can be worth it because aggregate throughput scales with N, benefiting bandwidth-heavy manycore workloads. A common misconception: equating lower hop count with higher throughput. They are related but different: throughput is about how many packets can cross a bisection simultaneously, not just the distance a single packet travels. Takeaway: quantify hops, pipeline cycles, buffer sizes and link counts to compare designs objectively for your target workload.

keyIdea.text: Latency = hops × pipeline cycles; throughput ≈ bisection bandwidth; power and area increase with routers, links and buffer sizes.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.1 › Design Trade-offs
Latency, Throughput, Power and Area Trade-offs
Make trade-offs explicit with simple formulas and counts.
Latency
Depends on hops and router pipeline cycles: latency ≈ hops × (router cycles + link cycles). Example: mesh average hops ≈ O(√N).
Throughput
Driven by bisection bandwidth. Mesh offers O(√N) links across the bisection, ring offers constant bandwidth.
Power & Area
Grow with number of routers, buffer entries and link lengths. More VCs increase buffer area and dynamic power.
Design checklist
  • Estimate average hops for your topology and N.
  • Count links across the bisection to approximate throughput scaling.
  • Compute total buffer bits to estimate area and power impact.

screens.title: Flow Control: Credit-Based and On/Off
screens.narratorSegment: Flow control keeps senders from overrunning receiver buffers. Two common approaches are credit-based and on/off. In credit-based flow control the sender keeps a count of available buffer slots at the receiver; a flit is transmitted only if the sender has credits, and credits are returned when the receiver frees space. This prevents buffer overflow with precise bookkeeping and supports fine-grained flow control. On/off flow control uses a simpler signal: a receiver notifies the sender to pause when it is full and resumes when space becomes available. On/off is simpler but less efficient under high utilization because it blocks larger classes of traffic and wastes link bandwidth. A misconception is that on/off is always cheaper; while it is simpler in control, its inefficiency under sustained traffic can increase latency and reduce throughput. Concrete example: in a router with multiple VCs, credit-based control allows per-VC credit tracking so one VC's stalls do not necessarily block others, while on/off signaling might halt all VCs on a link. Takeaway: prefer credit-based flow control for high-performance designs where buffer usage must be precisely managed; use on/off only where simplicity and low control cost are paramount.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.1 › Flow Control
Flow Control: Credit-Based and On/Off
Prevent buffer overflow and regulate link usage.
Credit-based flow control
Sender tracks available buffer slots at receiver. A flit is sent only if sender has credit. Precise and efficient under high utilization.
Good for
High-performance NoCs and per-VC accounting to avoid interference across flows.
On/off flow control
Receiver signals sender to stop or continue when buffer fullness crosses a threshold. Simple but less efficient under sustained load.
Good for
Simple designs with low traffic or where control complexity must be minimal.
Example scenario
If VC0 is full and uses credit-based flow control, only VC0's sender stalls; other VCs with credits continue. With on/off, the whole link may pause, reducing pipeline utilization.

screens.title: NoC Power Management Techniques
screens.narratorSegment: Power management in NoCs uses several familiar techniques adapted to interconnect hardware. Clock gating can stop router logic when there is no traffic, saving dynamic switching power. Voltage-frequency scaling lets the NoC run at reduced voltage and frequency under light traffic, cutting both dynamic and static power. Power gating can turn off unused routers or clusters when workloads are localized, saving leakage power at the cost of state retention and wakeup complexity. A misconception is that aggressive power gating is always beneficial; frequent switching between power states can increase wakeup latency and cause performance hiccups for latency-sensitive traffic. Practical example: in a workload where traffic is bursty and concentrated in a few clusters, power-gating idle routers in quiet regions plus clock gating active routers between bursts can reduce energy without harming performance. Design trade-offs include managing state (buffers and VC state) during gating, and ensuring flow-control prevents lost flits. Takeaway: combine techniques based on workload characteristics and tolerance for wakeup latency; test with realistic traffic patterns to choose gating thresholds and DVFS points. NoC Power Management Techniques means clock gating, dvfs and power gating reduce noc energy but introduce complexity in state retention and wakeup latency.. In practical terms, clock gating, dvfs and power gating in routers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 12 › Chapter 12.1 › NoC Power Management
NoC Power Management Techniques
Reduce energy while preserving performance when possible.
Clock gating
Gate clocks to router logic when idle to cut dynamic power with minimal state impact.
DVFS
Scale voltage and frequency to match traffic demand; saves dynamic and some static power at lower performance modes.
Power gating
Power off unused routers or clusters to eliminate leakage, but manage state retention and wakeup latency.
Design considerations
  • Balance energy saved with wakeup costs and added control logic.
  • Set gating thresholds using real traffic traces to avoid frequent transitions.
  • Plan for flow-control and state preservation when gating routers or ports.

screens.title: Designing a 4×4 Mesh Router — Calculation and XY Routing
screens.narratorSegment: Now we walk through the hands-on design and calculations. The target router has 5 ports, 2 virtual channels per port, and 4 flits per VC. Each flit is 128 bits. First, compute total buffer bits per router using ports × VCs × flits × flit width, which yields 5 × 2 × 4 × 128 = 5,120 bits per router and 81,920 bits for the 16 routers in a 4×4 mesh. Next, pick a switch allocator: round-robin is a simple fair choice that cycles grants among contenders to avoid starvation. For path tracing we use XY routing: packets first travel in X until the destination column, then in Y. To route from (0,0) to (3,3) the packet moves east three times then north three times, visiting four routers along X and then the final three along Y — count hops carefully: from node (0,0) to (3,3) the number of hops equals |Δx| + |Δy| = 6. For latency, assume lookahead routing gives 2 cycles per router and each link traversal costs 1 cycle. End-to-end latency is roughly hops × (2 cycles router + 1 cycle link) with overlap considerations; with lookahead you can often save one router cycle per hop due to overlap. Common mistake is to forget VC allocation at each hop: at every router the packet must secure a VC and a switch grant before traversal. Takeaway: arithmetic plus stepwise tracing yields an accurate design estimate and reveals where contention or deadlock risks appear.

Module 12 › Chapter 12.1 › Hands-on Design
Designing a 4×4 Mesh Router — Calculation and XY Routing
Stepwise arithmetic and a routing trace for a packet from (0,0) to (3,3).
Buffer sizing code block
// Parameters
ports = 5
vcs_per_port = 2
flits_per_vc = 4
flit_width_bits = 128

// Per-router calculation
buffer_bits_per_router = ports * vcs_per_port * flits_per_vc * flit_width_bits
// = 5 * 2 * 4 * 128 = 5120 bits

// Network-wide
num_routers = 16
total_buffer_bits = buffer_bits_per_router * num_routers
// = 16 * 5120 = 81920 bits
Round-robin switch allocator ensures fairness and bounded starvation risk; implement per-output arbitration rotating grants each cycle.
XY routing trace and latency
XY routing: move in X until correct column, then in Y. From (0,0) to (3,3): Δx=3, Δy=3 ⇒ hops=6.
// Latency parameters
router_cycles = 2  // with lookahead
link_cycles = 1
hops = 6

// Naive estimate
latency_cycles = hops * (router_cycles + link_cycles)
// = 6 * (2 + 1) = 18 cycles

// With lookahead overlaps, effective router cycles per hop may reduce; account for overlaps in detailed timing models.
Remember: each hop requires VC allocation and a switch grant; contention increases latency beyond the arithmetic estimate.

screens.title: Deadlock Scenario and How Virtual Channels Prevent It
screens.narratorSegment: Deadlock in NoCs occurs when a cycle of dependencies prevents forward progress: each packet waits for a resource held by the next packet in the cycle. A minimal deadlock example in a mesh is two adjacent nodes sending to each other simultaneously such that each holds a buffer needed by the other, or a four-way cycle where packets attempt to turn in a loop. To simulate this, consider two packets: A routed from (0,0) to (1,0) and B routed from (1,0) to (0,0). If both occupy the single VC on the connecting link and each waits for the other's buffer space, progress stalls. Virtual channels break this cycle by providing separate logical resources so that A uses VC0 and B uses VC1; since they do not share the same VC resource, the cyclic dependency is removed and at least one packet can advance. Another strategy is to assign VCs based on direction to prevent cycles in the resource dependency graph. Common misconception: deadlock only happens with many packets. In fact, cycles can appear with small numbers of packets under certain routing and buffering rules. Example: in an XY routing mesh, certain turn patterns can create cycles; plan VC allocation rules to eliminate those turns across VCs. Takeaway: identify the potential cycles in your dependency graph and assign VCs so that no cycle exists within a single VC network. How would you assign VCs to block all clockwise turning cycles in a 2D mesh?

keyIdea.title: Deadlock avoidance
keyIdea.text: Design VC allocation so resource dependency graphs have no cycles; separate traffic classes or directions across VCs to break potential deadlocks.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.1 › Deadlock and VCs
Deadlock Scenario and VC Prevention
A stepwise simulation of a circular wait and the VC-based fix.
Simulated deadlock steps
  1. Packet A at router R0 requests link to R1 and holds a buffer entry in VC0.
  2. Packet B at R1 requests link to R0 and holds a buffer entry in VC0 at R1.
  3. Each waits for the other’s buffer to free; no progress — a two-node cycle.
If only one VC exists per link this cycle locks both packets. With two VCs, assign A to VC0 and B to VC1 so each has independent buffering and credit bookkeeping and one can proceed.
VC assignment strategies
  • Separate request and reply flows into distinct VCs.
  • Assign VCs by direction to prevent cycles involving turns.
  • Ensure resource dependency graph per VC is acyclic.
Key Takeaway

Prevent deadlock by designing VC allocation rules so no cyclic buffer dependency can occur within a single VC network.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essentials. First, a NoC router comprises input buffers, route computation, a switch allocator and a crossbar; these building blocks together determine per-hop latency and throughput. Second, virtual channels create multiple logical buffers per physical link; they are essential for deadlock avoidance, QoS and reducing head-of-line blocking, but they increase buffer area and control complexity. Third, topology matters: rings are simple and fit small systems, meshes scale throughput and paths for manycore chips, crossbars are high bandwidth for small clusters, and hierarchical mixes balance local and global traffic. Remember to quantify design choices: compute buffer bits from ports, VCs, flits and flit width; estimate latency from hops and pipeline cycles; and evaluate throughput by counting bisection links. These are the practical levers you will use when designing or analyzing a NoC.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how on-chip networks connect cores and memories so that many cores can communicate efficiently. We will look closely at the NoC router as a tiny packet switch: its input buffers that hold flits, the route computation that picks an outgoing port, the switch allocator that resolves contention, and the crossbar that moves flits across the chip. You will also learn how virtual channels give multiple logical buffers per link to avoid deadlock and reduce head-of-line blocking. We will compare common topologies — ring, mesh, crossbar and hierarchical designs — and explain their trade-offs in latency, throughput, power and area. Finally, you will practice by designing a 4×4 mesh router with two virtual channels per port, calculating buffer sizes, tracing a packet with XY routing, computing latency with lookahead routing, and simulating a deadlock scenario and its resolution. By the end you will understand the concrete microarchitecture choices that determine on-chip performance and how to reason about the trade-offs when scaling to many cores. Which design choice will matter most for your chip’s workload?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to describe the main components inside a NoC router and explain how those parts interact to move packets. You will understand virtual channels: why multiple logical buffers exist per link, how they prevent deadlock, and how they reduce head-of-line blocking while supporting quality-of-service. You will be able to compare common NoC topologies — ring, mesh, crossbar and hierarchical hybrids — and state the latency, throughput and power trade-offs each one creates. Finally, you will be able to design a simple mesh router microarchitecture: choose buffer sizes, select a switch allocator scheme such as round-robin, and calculate latency for routed packets using the router pipeline and optional lookahead routing. These skills matter because they let you reason about scaling multicore systems, and they map directly to hardware design choices that affect performance and power. Think of these objectives as practical blueprints: explain, compare, analyze, and design.

This second objectives screen frames the skills as practical tasks you will perform. You will map router components to design choices: pick buffer depth for expected burstiness, choose allocator policies for fairness or priority, and decide whether to use output buffering or cut-through traversal. You will apply virtual channels to concrete problems: separate request and reply traffic, allocate dedicated VCs for high-priority flows, and reason about how two or more VCs per port affect area and complexity. For topology decisions you will quantify trade-offs: estimate how many hops a mesh route uses versus a ring, and how bisection bandwidth scales. Finally, in the design task you will calculate total buffer bits given number of ports, VCs, buffer depth, and flit width, then trace a packet through routers using XY routing and compute latency using the router pipeline plus link times. Each objective is tied to a measurable milestone so you can verify competency through simple design calculations and route traces.

A NoC router is the local traffic controller that moves flits from incoming links to outgoing links. At its simplest the router has input buffers where arriving flits are stored, a route computation unit that chooses an output port based on the packet destination and routing algorithm, a switch allocator that resolves contention when multiple inputs want the same output, and a crossbar that physically connects inputs to outputs for the transfer. Input buffers are sized to absorb bursts; a typical design uses 4–16 flits per input port. The switch allocator can use round-robin fairness or priority arbitration when latency-sensitive traffic exists. Crossbars are sized to the number of ports: for a 5-port router (north, south, east, west, local) a 5×5 crossbar provides full connectivity. Output buffers are optional — some designs use cut-through traversal to reduce latency by allowing flits to pass through without per-hop output buffering. An important misconception is to equate larger buffers with always better performance. In practice, larger buffers increase area and power and can hide backpressure poorly; sizing is a trade-off informed by expected traffic burstiness. Example: a router receiving short bursts from four neighbors benefits from moderate input buffers and a fair allocator to avoid starvation. Key takeaway: understand each block’s role so you can balance latency, throughput and area when sizing buffers and picking arbitration policies. How would you change buffer depth if burstiness doubled?

Routers commonly implement a simple pipeline to structure work and meet timing. The three-stage pipeline is: Buffer Write where an incoming flit is stored in an input buffer, Route Computation combined with Switch Allocation where the next-hop output and the switch grant are decided, and Switch Traversal plus Link Traversal where the flit crosses the crossbar and enters the physical link to the next router. This pipeline ensures predictable throughput but introduces per-hop latency. Lookahead routing is an optimization where a router computes the route for the next hop before the flit arrives at that hop. With lookahead, the downstream router can start its allocation in parallel, effectively reducing the pipeline depth seen per hop. For example, a design that normally takes three cycles per hop might be reduced to two cycles per hop with lookahead for single-flit packets. A common misconception is that lookahead always reduces latency without cost. In practice, lookahead increases control complexity and may require extra wiring or speculative state. Concrete example: with two-cycle-per-router lookahead and one cycle per link, a packet traversing 6 hops would take roughly 6×(2+1) minus lookahead overlaps; we reason carefully about overlaps when computing end-to-end latency. Takeaway: pipeline stages and lookahead trade simplicity for per-hop latency; choose based on packet sizes and timing budgets.

Virtual channels (VCs) are multiple logical buffers multiplexed over a single physical link. Each VC has its own buffer and flow-control state, which means we can separate traffic classes or protocol directions without adding extra physical wires. VCs solve several problems. First, they avoid deadlock by separating traffic into virtual networks that do not form cyclic dependencies; for example, separating request and reply packets into distinct VCs prevents a cycle where each packet waits on buffers held by the other. Second, VCs enable quality-of-service: a high-priority flow can use a dedicated VC so that low-priority traffic does not block it. Third, VCs reduce head-of-line blocking because if one VC's head flit is blocked, other VCs on the same physical link can still make progress. A typical router uses two to four VCs per input port. A common misconception is to treat VCs as a free win; in practice they increase area, buffering requirements and control complexity. Concrete example: two-packet deadlock where packets swap directions on adjacent routers can be resolved by allocating distinct VCs for those directions. Takeaway: VCs are a powerful, well-understood tool for deadlock avoidance and performance isolation, but they cost area and design complexity, so pick the number of VCs based on workload needs and power budgets.

When you add virtual channels you change the router’s buffering structure: each input port now contains multiple VCs, and each VC has its own buffer and flow-control state. A typical design uses two to four VCs per input port; each VC buffer depth is often 4–16 flits depending on burstiness. Buffer sizing affects area and power directly because more buffer entries mean more SRAM or register file resources. To ground this, consider the hands-on design: a 4×4 mesh has 16 nodes. Each router in our example has 5 ports (north, south, east, west, local), 2 VCs per port, and 4 flits per VC. If one flit is 128 bits wide, calculate total buffer bits per router by multiplying ports × VCs × depth × flit width. Many students forget to multiply by the number of ports when counting buffers; this omission underestimates area and power. Practical tip: compute the per-router total and then scale to the full network to estimate aggregate buffer memory. Example calculation: 5 ports × 2 VCs × 4 flits × 128 bits = 5,120 bits per router. If you then multiply across 16 routers you get the full chip buffer bits. Key takeaway: buffer sizing is straightforward arithmetic but decisive for area and power budgets; always account for ports, VCs and flit width together.

Selecting a NoC topology is a central design decision. A ring is simple and has low router count, so it can be efficient for small systems. However, its bandwidth across any bisection remains small, which limits throughput as the core count grows. A mesh is regular and scales to many cores: routers tile the chip and links are relatively short, and the mesh offers multiple independent paths so aggregate throughput increases with size. Crossbars give full connectivity within small clusters and provide very high bandwidth at small scale, but they become impractical beyond a few cores due to area and wiring. Hierarchical designs combine local rings or crossbars with a global mesh to get the best of both: local low-latency clusters and scalable global interconnect. When comparing these topologies, consider latency, throughput, power, and area. Common misconception: assume the mesh always outperforms the ring. For small N a ring may have lower average latency and lower power. Example: for N=16 cores a ring can be efficient, but for N=64 a mesh's increased bisection bandwidth becomes critical. Takeaway: match topology to expected core count and communication patterns; use hierarchical mixes when both local and global traffic matter.

NoC design is a careful balance between latency, throughput, power and area. Latency depends on the average number of hops between source and destination and the router pipeline depth; meshes typically give O(√N) hops while rings can require O(N) hops. Throughput is governed by bisection bandwidth: meshes scale with the square root of the node count because multiple links cross the bisection, whereas a ring provides constant bisection bandwidth regardless of size. Power is driven by the number of routers, length and number of links, and the amount of buffering; meshes have more routers but shorter links, rings have fewer routers but longer links; both choices change dynamic and static power. Area is dominated by router logic and buffers — more VCs and deeper buffers increase area. Designers often trade a little extra latency for much higher throughput or lower power, depending on workload. For example, accepting O(√N) hops in a mesh can be worth it because aggregate throughput scales with N, benefiting bandwidth-heavy manycore workloads. A common misconception: equating lower hop count with higher throughput. They are related but different: throughput is about how many packets can cross a bisection simultaneously, not just the distance a single packet travels. Takeaway: quantify hops, pipeline cycles, buffer sizes and link counts to compare designs objectively for your target workload.

Flow control keeps senders from overrunning receiver buffers. Two common approaches are credit-based and on/off. In credit-based flow control the sender keeps a count of available buffer slots at the receiver; a flit is transmitted only if the sender has credits, and credits are returned when the receiver frees space. This prevents buffer overflow with precise bookkeeping and supports fine-grained flow control. On/off flow control uses a simpler signal: a receiver notifies the sender to pause when it is full and resumes when space becomes available. On/off is simpler but less efficient under high utilization because it blocks larger classes of traffic and wastes link bandwidth. A misconception is that on/off is always cheaper; while it is simpler in control, its inefficiency under sustained traffic can increase latency and reduce throughput. Concrete example: in a router with multiple VCs, credit-based control allows per-VC credit tracking so one VC's stalls do not necessarily block others, while on/off signaling might halt all VCs on a link. Takeaway: prefer credit-based flow control for high-performance designs where buffer usage must be precisely managed; use on/off only where simplicity and low control cost are paramount.

Power management in NoCs uses several familiar techniques adapted to interconnect hardware. Clock gating can stop router logic when there is no traffic, saving dynamic switching power. Voltage-frequency scaling lets the NoC run at reduced voltage and frequency under light traffic, cutting both dynamic and static power. Power gating can turn off unused routers or clusters when workloads are localized, saving leakage power at the cost of state retention and wakeup complexity. A misconception is that aggressive power gating is always beneficial; frequent switching between power states can increase wakeup latency and cause performance hiccups for latency-sensitive traffic. Practical example: in a workload where traffic is bursty and concentrated in a few clusters, power-gating idle routers in quiet regions plus clock gating active routers between bursts can reduce energy without harming performance. Design trade-offs include managing state (buffers and VC state) during gating, and ensuring flow-control prevents lost flits. Now we walk through the hands-on design and calculations. The target router has 5 ports, 2 virtual channels per port, and 4 flits per VC. Each flit is 128 bits. First, compute total buffer bits per router using ports × VCs × flits × flit width, which yields 5 × 2 × 4 × 128 = 5,120 bits per router and 81,920 bits for the 16 routers in a 4×4 mesh. Next, pick a switch allocator: round-robin is a simple fair choice that cycles grants among contenders to avoid starvation. For path tracing we use XY routing: packets first travel in X until the destination column, then in Y. To route from (0,0) to (3,3) the packet moves east three times then north three times, visiting four routers along X and then the final three along Y — count hops carefully: from node (0,0) to (3,3) the number of hops equals |Δx| + |Δy| = 6. For latency, assume lookahead routing gives 2 cycles per router and each link traversal costs 1 cycle. End-to-end latency is roughly hops × (2 cycles router + 1 cycle link) with overlap considerations; with lookahead you can often save one router cycle per hop due to overlap. Common mistake is to forget VC allocation at each hop: at every router the packet must secure a VC and a switch grant before traversal. Takeaway: arithmetic plus stepwise tracing yields an accurate design estimate and reveals where contention or deadlock risks appear.

Deadlock in NoCs occurs when a cycle of dependencies prevents forward progress: each packet waits for a resource held by the next packet in the cycle. A minimal deadlock example in a mesh is two adjacent nodes sending to each other simultaneously such that each holds a buffer needed by the other, or a four-way cycle where packets attempt to turn in a loop. To simulate this, consider two packets: A routed from (0,0) to (1,0) and B routed from (1,0) to (0,0). If both occupy the single VC on the connecting link and each waits for the other's buffer space, progress stalls. Virtual channels break this cycle by providing separate logical resources so that A uses VC0 and B uses VC1; since they do not share the same VC resource, the cyclic dependency is removed and at least one packet can advance. Another strategy is to assign VCs based on direction to prevent cycles in the resource dependency graph. Common misconception: deadlock only happens with many packets. In fact, cycles can appear with small numbers of packets under certain routing and buffering rules. Example: in an XY routing mesh, certain turn patterns can create cycles; plan VC allocation rules to eliminate those turns across VCs. Takeaway: identify the potential cycles in your dependency graph and assign VCs so that no cycle exists within a single VC network. Let's summarize the essentials. First, a NoC router comprises input buffers, route computation, a switch allocator and a crossbar; these building blocks together determine per-hop latency and throughput. Second, virtual channels create multiple logical buffers per physical link; they are essential for deadlock avoidance, QoS and reducing head-of-line blocking, but they increase buffer area and control complexity. Third, topology matters: rings are simple and fit small systems, meshes scale throughput and paths for manycore chips, crossbars are high bandwidth for small clusters, and hierarchical mixes balance local and global traffic. Remember to quantify design choices: compute buffer bits from ports, VCs, flits and flit width; estimate latency from hops and pipeline cycles; and evaluate throughput by counting bisection links.
